clue.text: Girl about a hundred pursued by a joker, the rogue!

indicators.note: the joker follows on behind the girl, so comes after her in the answer
the girl's name is wrapped about the numeral, so it goes inside

parts.note: Sally is a girl's name
C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
a wag is a joker or wit

explanation.surface: An exclamation at a rascal who chased a girl with a hundred jokes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' places the numeral inside the girl's name, and 'pursued by' means the joker comes after her in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A scamp or mischievous rascal is a synonym of rogue.

clue.text: Dark mill owner solves the unemployment problem

definitions.text: Dark mill owner solves the unemployment problem

parts.words: Dark mill owner solves the unemployment problem
parts.note: recalls Blake's 'dark ... mills' and the saying that the Devil finds work for idle hands

explanation.definitionFit: The Devil owns the dark mills of Blake's hymn and finds mischief for the idle, so he is the employer.

clue.text: Pleasant results when we site a mine differently

indicators.note: the words are sited differently, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Mining engineers are told that moving a mine elsewhere will bring benefits.
explanation.walkthrough: 'we' is only a link; the nine letters of 'site a mine' make the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Pleasant features or facilities of a place are its comforts and conveniences.

clue.text: Sacked though game to make hay

parts.note: loo is an old card game
to ted is to spread mown grass out to dry for hay

explanation.surface: Raiders ransacked a farm yet still had the energy to make hay.
explanation.walkthrough: LOO is an old gambling card game, and to TED is a farming verb for turning hay.
explanation.definitionFit: A town that is plundered has been looted, just as one that is sacked.

clue.text: Coastal clean-up

parts.note: the surge of waves along a shore, and also a cleaning

explanation.definitionFit: Waves rush over a beach, and a scrub with water cleans something.

clue.text: Down -to — earth sources of Whitman's verse

explanation.surface: Praise for the earthy origins of an American poet's lines.
explanation.walkthrough: Walt Whitman's verse collection is 'Leaves of Grass', so its sources are the roots of grass.
explanation.definitionFit: Ordinary people at the base of a movement are down to earth; Whitman's 'Leaves of Grass' springs from grass.

clue.text: Doesn't the best man eat noisily?

explanation.surface: A question about wedding manners at the reception table.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the best man' is not the groom's helper but the top competitor, short for champion; to champ is to munch noisily.
explanation.definitionFit: A champion is the best competitor; to chomp loudly with the jaws is to champ.

clue.text: But typewriters' ribbons don't help to drive it

definitions.text: But typewriters' ribbons don't help to drive it

parts.words: But typewriters' ribbons don't help to drive it
parts.note: ribbons are a coachman's reins, which drive a horse vehicle, but a typewriter's inked ribbon does not move its moving part

explanation.definitionFit: Both a horse-drawn vehicle and the sliding part of a typewriter go by this name.

clue.text: Turks inhabit it back in Canada

indicators.note: the letters run back through the word, from right to left
the answer lies in the word Canada

explanation.surface: Turkish people living back in Canada.
explanation.walkthrough: Reading Canada backwards gives ADANAC, and the city's letters sit inside that.
explanation.definitionFit: A city in southern Turkey is home to Turkish people.

clue.text: Are they, all good-lookers, these fine ladies?

definitions.text: Are they, all good-lookers, these fine ladies?

parts.words: Are they, all good-lookers, these fine ladies?
parts.note: to peer is to look, so women who peer would be lookers, and the female peers of the realm are fine ladies

explanation.definitionFit: Noblewomen holding titles are fine ladies, and the word also suggests women who peer or look.

clue.text: No great shakes

parts.note: read literally, small shakings of the ground rather than the idiom for something unremarkable

explanation.definitionFit: Small earthquakes or quivers are literally shakes that are not great.

clue.text: Old town, its duration and extent

parts.note: Acre is an ancient port town in present-day Israel
an age is a long duration of time

explanation.surface: A history guide describing an ancient town's long life and size.
explanation.definitionFit: Land area measured in acres gives its size or extent.

clue.text: We hear them — one is in things that are blown

indicators.note: the numeral is in the blown things, so it goes inside them

parts.note: noses are what you blow into a handkerchief
I is the Roman numeral one

explanation.surface: A riddle about things blown, like trumpets, that we can hear.
explanation.walkthrough: 'things that are blown' suggests wind instruments, but it is noses.
explanation.definitionFit: Sounds are things heard, so the clue's 'We hear them' describes them.

clue.text: Reckon I'm to come into landed property

indicators.note: the speaker is to come into the property, so goes inside it

parts.note: an estate is a large holding of land
taken as its letters, without the apostrophe

explanation.surface: Someone working out what an inheritance of land will be worth.
explanation.walkthrough: 'come into' looks like inheriting land, but 'to come into' is the container signal for the two letters of I'm.
explanation.definitionFit: To judge a figure roughly is to reckon or calculate it.

clue.text: For example in a league it is a duty

indicators.note: the abbreviation goes in the league word

parts.note: an alliance is a league of allies

explanation.surface: A rule saying, for example, that within a league one has a duty.
explanation.definitionFit: Loyalty owed to a ruler or country is a duty.

clue.text: Mother loses a ton and floats

annotationWithheld.why: Mother loses a ton and floats (4): no parse found from 'Mother' minus a ton to SHIP; perhaps MOTHERSHIP is meant, but nothing removes MOTHER, so the wordplay is unclear
annotationWithheld.clue: Mother loses a ton and floats

clue.text: Comestible of commotion

parts.note: a food whose name, split in two, describes fuss and bustle

explanation.walkthrough: The answer is an Irish porridge; split into 'stir about' it means a commotion.
explanation.definitionFit: Oatmeal porridge is a food, and its name also means a fuss or bustle.

clue.text: Open these and the issue is unlikely to be 16

definitions.text: Open these and the issue is unlikely to be 16

parts.words: Open these and the issue is unlikely to be 16
parts.note: opening the sluices lets water out in a rush, not slowly, with 16 the answer to 16-down

explanation.definitionFit: Sluice barriers hold back a river, and the outflow when they open is a torrent rather than a dribble.

clue.text: Just flowing enough to deceive fish

parts.note: to trick someone is to deceive them
the ling is a long fish of the cod family

explanation.surface: A stream with barely enough water to fool the fish.
explanation.definitionFit: Water that is barely running, in a thin stream, is just flowing.

clue.text: Reporters subjected to the pull of party members

definitions.text: Reporters subjected to the pull of party members

parts.words: Reporters subjected to the pull of party members
parts.note: reporters are things that go bang, and partygoers pull them at Christmas

explanation.walkthrough: 'Reporters' are not journalists but bangers; Christmas party novelties go off with a report when two people pull them.
explanation.definitionFit: Party novelties that snap with a bang when pulled are the reporters of the clue.

clue.text: Can't quite cover gentlemen against risks from rebels

indicators.note: the cover is not quite complete, so its final letter is dropped

parts.note: to insure is to cover, as with a policy against risks
gents is short for gentlemen

explanation.surface: An insurer unable to cover gentlemen against the dangers that rebels pose.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Can't quite' cuts INSURE to INSUR; 'against risks' only completes the insurance sense of 'cover' in the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Insurgents are people rising in revolt, so rebels.

clue.text: They control horsepower, but not wholly

explanation.surface: A remark about engines that only partly manage their horsepower.
explanation.walkthrough: 'horsepower' is read as the power of horses, which mouthpieces in their jaws control; 'not wholly' means in parts or pieces, as in 'bits and pieces'.
explanation.definitionFit: Metal mouthpieces steer horses; pieces or fragments are not the whole.

clue.text: Fruit in hand

parts.note: a bunch of this fruit growing together is called a hand

explanation.definitionFit: A cluster of this curved yellow fruit is known as a hand.

clue.text: Bright in the top-storey, one who has this ?

definitions.text: Bright in the top-storey, one who has this ?

parts.words: Bright in the top-storey, one who has this ?
parts.note: a clever head is a bright top storey, and the top storey of a house is its loft

explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means refined Athenian-style humour, while the loft pun gives a sharp mind upstairs.

clue.text: A rose for Mary

parts.note: the emblem rose of a royal house, and the surname of Queen Mary I

explanation.definitionFit: Mary I belonged to the royal house whose emblem is a red-and-white rose.

clue.text: A care, might one say, of Dombey's man ?

definitions.text: A care, might one say, of Dombey's man ?

parts.words: A care, might one say, of Dombey's man ?
parts.note: to cark is an old word for to worry, and Dombey's manager in Dickens has this name

explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's 'Dombey and Son', James Carker is Mr Dombey's scheming manager; 'cark' is an archaic word for care or anxiety.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dickens villain who manages Dombey's firm carries a surname that sounds like one who worries.

clue.text: Speeds to make you stare

indicators.note: the letters of the word stare are made over into another word

explanation.surface: Speeds high enough to make you stare in amazement.
explanation.definitionFit: Paces of travel are speeds, as in rates of knots.

clue.text: Does it stiffen the upper lip that's bitten, the dust?

definitions.text: Does it stiffen the upper lip that's bitten, the dust?

parts.words: Does it stiffen the upper lip that's bitten, the dust?
parts.note: courage gives a stiff upper lip, and fine dust or sand is bitten in falling

explanation.definitionFit: Courage and small particles of sand share the name.

clue.text: Wooster as superannuated runner ?

parts.note: Bertie Wooster's form of address for a friend, read as an aged runner-type vegetable

explanation.walkthrough: Bertie Wooster, of P G Wodehouse's stories, calls his chums this; a runner bean is a climbing bean, so an elderly one fits.
explanation.definitionFit: The chummy greeting of an upper-class Englishman doubles as a pod vegetable past its prime.

clue.text: An Asian in rest is no dreamer

indicators.note: the Asian goes in the word rest

parts.note: taken as written
Ali is a common name in Asia

explanation.surface: An Asian at rest is a practical person, not a dreamer.
explanation.definitionFit: A pragmatist who sees things as they are is the opposite of a dreamer.

clue.text: A wild spurt of the spirit of painting

indicators.note: a wild spurt is one thrown about, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: An artist's brush spurts wildly with the energy of painting.
explanation.definitionFit: Turpentine, a spirit used to thin oil paint, is shortened in speech.

clue.text: Offers cold shoulder owing to wrongly set cookers

indicators.note: the word set is placed wrongly, so its letters come out rearranged

parts.note: ranges are large kitchen stoves

explanation.surface: A cook falls out with someone because ovens were installed badly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wrongly' rearranges the three letters of 'set', and 'owing to' is only a link to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To alienate someone is to turn them away, giving them the cold shoulder.
